abstract: The paper gives a brief history of systems of electrical unite with emphasis on the factors that have led to the development of m.k.s. units and of the rationalization of units. The functioning of the m.k.s. system is treated in detail on the basis of the more familiar c.g.s. systems of units, and the rationalization of the system of units is explained. Finally the c.g.s. and m.k.s. systems are compared from points of view of use in electromagnetic theory, in education and in electrical engineering practice.

articleTitle: The development of broadcasting in the union of South Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The mere quoting of historical data usually makes poor reading and cannot be of much interest in its presentation. I will therefore attempt to trace the development with a minimum of historical reference but, as the development has been so much a part of the history of broadcasting and vice versa, it is impossible to avoid historical reference entirely. Broadcasting in the Union actually came into being as a result of the British Empire Exhibition of 1924. The original 1-kW medium-frequency installation in Johannesburg was used to raise funds on behalf of the South African section of the above exhibition. The local committee was formed by the South African Railways and Harbours Administration. Press reports towards the end of November 1923 stated that broadcasting was about to come to the Hand and that ' bright programmes could be expected during December.' The first concert was timed for 18th December 1923, and the late General Smuts opened the proceedings from the Roberts Heights Hospital by speaking over a then conventional post office telephone circuit which was coupled in Johannesburg to the transmitter input.

articleTitle: Some recent developments in electric motors, with special reference to the use of new insulation materials
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: General trends in the design of a.c. motors are discussed, and attention is drawn to the increasing popularity of the t.e.f.c. motor. Particular mention is made of the problems of internal cooling, and a successful design is described. The method of eliminating condensation inside the machine is outlined. The problem of low-current direct-start motors is touched upon and the alternative designs of rotors discussed. General trends in d.c. motor design indicates a situation similar to the above, and a typical t.e.c.a.c. machine is mentioned. The present position on motor standardization in England is recorded. Improvements in machine insulation are dealt with for both Class A and Class B machines. Varnish treatments are discussed and attention drawn to the rarely mentioned feature of moisture absorption by the windings due to the permeability of varnish films. The improvements in magnetic sheet steel are noted, and reference is made to the possible use of the new cold-rolled directional steels. Ball and roller bearings are discussed with particular reference to oil or grease lubrication. Pump drives raise special problems in alignment and end location of rotors. Some a.c. motor troubles are mentioned.

abstract: The paper tends to discount the lost-call theory of on-demand systems with so-called non-waiting arrangements, as well as the grade of service conception deduced therefrom. In its place an outlook is offered based on an appreciation of traffic theory which provides a set of continuous relationships covering the practical problems produced in any on-demand as well as any trunk-line system. The whole sphere cannot be covered adequately in one paper and for reasons of general interest the paper has been limited in mathematical argument. The basic traffic theory has perforce had to be reviewed to build up the outlook.

articleTitle: The work of the bernard price institute of geophysical research, 1938-1951
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is a very great privilege to be asked by the Institute to deliver the first Bernard Price Memorial Lecture. On this occasion we honour the memory and we recall the achievements of one who was perhaps the greatest President our Institute has had. As an electrical engineer and as the head of the Victoria Falls and Transvaal Power Company, Dr Bernard Price devoted the last forty years of his life — the most productive and important period of his career — to the service of this country. His wise management, his engineering ability and his foresight in planning contributed in considerable measure to the progress of our mining industry and to our general industrial development. The widespread network of power lines which to-day crosses the Transvaal and the Northern Free State and the great power stations which feed them are to a very large extent his creation and stand to-day as his monument for all to see.

articleTitle: Some technical considerations relating to the design, performance and application of high-voltage sw1tchgear
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper discusses six technical considerations relating to high-voltage switchgear. Section 2 deals with rate of rise of restriking voltage (r.r.r.v) : it draws attention to the difficulty of assessing the severity of double-frequency transients and the importance of making a correct estimate of running conditions. It is concluded that r.r.r.v can be calculated with sufficient accuracy for practical purposes. The way in which the performance of a circuit-breaker is affected by r.r.r.v is discussed in Section 3. It is shown, for example, that air-break circuit-breakers are hardly affected ; oil-break circuit-breakers are affected only at small currents ; and air-blast circuit-breakers may be affected over a relatively wide range of currents. Section 4 discusses the effects of current chopping when switching small reactive currents, and shows how the overvoltage varies with the r.m.s. value of the current and with the earthing of the neutral point.

abstract: RobertHowe-Gould,who died on 26thAugust, 1951, was born in London in 1877 and educated in Berlin. In 1896 he came to South Africa for Siemens and Halske and was responsible for the erection of some of the earliest threephase plants in the country. He also designed and erected power and lighting plants for several of the early goldmines, collieries and towns in the Transvaal, notable amongwhich were the Dynamite Factory at Modderfontein, the Lan caster Gold Mining Company, T.G.M.E. atPilgrim’sRest and the lighting of the suburbs of Johannes burg.
